TG Therapeutics (TGTX) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Hospital uptake peaked as a subcutaneous version moves toward quarterly dosing.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

TG Therapeutics, Inc. (TGTX +5.94%) reported a quarter of growth across its commercial and clinical operations, highlighted by the raising of its full-year global revenue guidance to 1 billion. Management stated that the company generated 85.9 million in operating income, supported by an expansion in the use of BRIUMVI among treatment-naive patients and younger demographics. The company focused on its capital allocation strategy by repurchasing 100 million of its common stock while maintaining a cash position of 556.7 million. Strategic development remains centered on life cycle innovations for BRIUMVI, including a simplified intravenous initiation dose and a subcutaneous formulation, alongside the advancement of its allogeneic CAR T cell therapy for progressive multiple sclerosis.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the TG Therapeutics Third Quarter 2026 Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note, this conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the call over to your host, Jenna Bosco, Chief Communications Officer. Please go ahead.

Jenna Bosco: Thank you. Welcome, everyone, and thank you for joining us this morning. I'm Jenna Bosco, and with me to discuss TG Therapeutics' Third Quarter 2026 financial results are Michael Weiss, our Chairman and Chief Executive Officer; Hari Miskin, our Chief Development Officer; Adam Waldman, our Chief Commercial Officer; and Sean Power, our Chief Financial Officer. Following our safe harbor statement, Mike will begin with an overview of our recent corporate developments. Hari will then discuss highlights from our recent data presentation, followed by Adam, who will provide an update on our commercial efforts. Sean will conclude our prepared remarks with a review of our financial results before we open the call for Q&A.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind everyone that today's discussion will include forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These statements may include expectations regarding our future operating and financial performance, including sales trends, revenue guidance, projected milestones, development plans and the outlook for our marketed products and our pipeline products. Please note that these statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that can cause our actual results to differ materially from those indicated. These risks are detailed in our SEC filings. Additionally, any forward-looking statements made today reflect our views only as of this date, and we disclaim any obligation to update or revise them.

As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded and will be available for replay for the next 30 days on our website at www.tgtherapeutics.com. With that, I'll now turn the call over to Mike Weiss, our CEO.

Michael Weiss: Thank you, Jenna, and good morning, everyone. We appreciate you joining us today. I'm pleased to report another strong quarter for TG with meaningful progress across both our commercial business and development programs. Global revenue for the quarter was approximately $260 million, including $233 million in U.S. BRIUMVI net revenue. With solid third quarter performance and trends pointing to a strong fourth quarter, we're raising our full year global revenue guidance to $1 billion for 2026, a pretty remarkable accomplishment less than four years after launching BRIUMVI. I'd like to pause here to congratulate our team for their hard work and dedication to the MS community and to TG.

And as they know, we're just getting started. $1 billion in annual revenue is an important milestone, but I don't believe it comes close to defining the opportunity ahead of us. On our last call, I described BRIUMVI as a starting line for TG, providing the commercial capabilities, financial resources and scientific foundation to build a value creation engine. And I think the progress we've made over the last several months offers a compelling example of what that means. And nowhere was that progress more evident than at this year's ECTRIMS meeting in Toronto.

We presented an extensive collection of data ranging from seven-year clinical outcomes to new real-world evidence, life cycle innovations and the first clinical results from azer-cel and progressive MS. Given the breadth of these presentations, I thought it would be valuable for investors to hear directly from our Chief Development Officer, Hari Miskin, who will take you through the key findings shortly. But first, I wanted to share some of my own observations from the conference. I had the opportunity to meet with over 100 physicians and advanced practice providers during the conference. Conversation after conversation reinforced just how far we've come and the growing appreciation for the value BRIUMVI and TG are bringing to the MS community.

I was particularly encouraged by the growing recognition that not all anti-CD20 therapies are the same and that those differences may translate into meaningful differences in the treatment experience. What I found most interesting is how the data from ENHANCE and ENABLE are reinforcing some of these differences observed in clinical practice. And when clinical evidence meets personal experience, adoption follows. For me, that's how we'll achieve our ambition of becoming the most prescribed anti-CD20 therapy among new MS treatment starts. We believe two important innovations can help accelerate our progress toward that goal, the consolidated IV initiation dose and self-administered subcu BRIUMVI.

The first, which was studied in our positive Phase III ENHANCE study, would simplify the initiation of IV BRIUMVI by combining the day 1 and day 15 initiation doses into a single infusion. If approved, BRIUMVI will be the only IV anti-CD20 that offers the simplicity of a single initiation infusion followed every six months by a one-hour maintenance infusion. We believe that combination could represent a meaningful competitive advantage for IV BRIUMVI. In terms of timing, we're still targeting a potential approval of this new initiation dosing around mid-2027. The other subcu BRIUMVI represents our biggest near-term growth opportunity.

Today, approximately 35% of new anti-CD20 treatment starts are for patients choosing self-administration, a market in which BRIUMVI doesn't currently participate. And we believe this segment alone represents a multibillion-dollar opportunity. But here is what makes the opportunity particularly attractive to TG. We're not starting from scratch. We already have an established brand, a growing physician network and a commercial infrastructure serving the same MS community. And with the potential for quarterly self-administration, we believe subcu BRIUMVI could offer a compelling alternative to existing treatment options that require more frequent dosing. With Phase III results expected around year-end or early 2027, we're working toward a potential launch in 2028.

And strategically, we see subcu as additive to our IV business, not a replacement for it. Our goal is to make BRIUMVI a compelling treatment option regardless of how patients prefer to receive therapy because we believe no patient should have to choose their treatment solely based on route of administration. Beyond these life cycle innovations, TRS also offered an early glimpse of what could become an entirely new frontier in MS treatment, CAR T cell therapy. We are pleased to present the first clinical results from azer-cel, our allogeneic CAR T in progressive MS, where there remains a significant unmet medical need. Let me close with where I see TG today and where we are going.

We're delivering on our commercial commitments, raising our outlook and building a business that we believe has the potential to become substantially larger than it is today. And importantly, we don't believe our opportunities end with BRIUMVI in relapsing MS. We're exploring entirely new treatment approaches, including azer-cel and progressive MS, while advancing BRIUMVI in myasthenia gravis, treatment-resistant schizophrenia and potentially other indications. Each of these programs represents an opportunity to create additional value beyond our existing business. and we're pursuing them from a position of increasing financial strength. At the same time, we're committed to being disciplined with the capital we're generating.

Our objective remains clear: to build a company capable of repeatedly creating value through scientific innovation, disciplined execution and thoughtful investments that generate attractive long-term returns. I'm proud of what we've accomplished. But when I consider the opportunities in front of us, I believe we're still early in the stages of what TG can become. With that, I'll turn the call over to our Chief Development Officer, Hari Miskin, for a closer look at the clinical results from ECTRIMS and an overview of our development programs. Hari, welcome to the call.

Unknown Executive: Thank you, Mike, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to join you all today to provide an update on our clinical development programs and highlights of our recently presented data. As Mike mentioned, ECTRIMS was a particularly productive meeting for TG, the largest in the company's history in terms of the breadth and depth of data shared with presentations highlighting long-term outcomes of BRIUMVI, continued differentiation versus others in the class, progress across our life cycle programs and encouraging initial results from azer-cel in progressive MS. I'll begin with BRIUMVI, where investigators at ECTRIMS presented seven-year follow-up results from the ULTIMATE clinical development program. These results continue to demonstrate sustained efficacy.

Among patients who completed seven years of continuous BRIUMVI treatment, the annualized relapse rate was 0.018, roughly one relapse in over 50 patient years and approximately 88% remained free of 24-week confirmed display progression. To our knowledge, this is an unprecedented level of freedom from disability progression in longer-term follow-up studies originating from Phase III relapsing MS trials. The safety findings were also reassuring with no new safety signals observed over seven years of treatment. Together, these results reinforce our confidence in BRIUMVI as a long-term treatment option for people living with relapsing MS. We also presented updated real-world findings from ENABLE, our ongoing U.S. Phase IV observational study, which now includes more than 1,000 patients.

The results continue to reinforce the clinical profile we saw in our registration trials. 99% of patients remained relapse-free. Infusion times were consistent with our approved one-hour maintenance infusion and rates of infusion-related reactions were lower than those observed in the registrational trials. Turning to ENHANCE. This Phase IIb study initially focused on evaluating switches to BRIUMVI from prior anti-CD20 therapy and has evolved over time to also explore alternate dosing regimens for BRIUMVI, yielding a number of valuable data sets. The study culminated in a randomized trial to evaluate consolidating our approved two-dose initiation regimen into a single 600-milligram initiation infusion with the goal of making treatment initiation more convenient for patients and providers.

The trial met its primary endpoint, demonstrating bioequivalence between the two regimens. Importantly, day one infusion-related reactions were numerically lower with the single-dose initiation regimen, 16% compared to approximately 26% for the standard regimen with no grade 3 or higher infusion-related reactions in either arm. B-cell depletion and MRI outcomes were also comparable for both regimens. Together, these findings support the potential to simplify BRIUMVI initiation without compromising drug exposure or the observed safety profile. We are advancing the regulatory process and subject to approval, anticipate a potential update to our label to incorporate this new regimen around the middle of 2027.

We also presented an update on an earlier cohort from the ENHANCE study, which enrolled over 100 patients who transitioned directly from ocrelizumab to BRIUMVI. Approximately 60% of these patients reported experiencing wearing off symptoms while on ocrelizumab. However, following the transition to BRIUMVI, nearly 70% did not report this wearing off effect through week 48 of treatment. Interestingly, this switch cohort also contained a number of patients who experienced incomplete B-cell depletion or early reactants on ocrelizumab, yet we were able to obtain robust B-cell depletion with BRIUMVI. We believe these findings further support the potential for meaningful biological differences among anti-CD20 therapies, and we intend to continue investigating these observations and their potential clinical significance.

On that note, it's worth noting a recent publication in the journal Multiple Sclerosis and Related Disorders, which was a five-year comparative analysis of ublituximab against both ocrelizumab and ofatumumab. This peer-reviewed publication used an unanchored match-adjusted methodology to account for differences between the clinical trial populations to provide a statistically valid comparison. The findings were particularly interesting. Ublituximab was associated with a 44% lower estimated risk of confirmed 24-week disability progression compared with ocrelizumab and a 49% lower risk compared with ofatumumab. While these findings come from an indirect comparison rather than a randomized head-to-head trial, we believe the consistency of the results against both leading anti-CD20 therapies is thought-provoking and warrants further investigation. Now turning to subcu BRIUMVI.

The Phase I results presented at ECTRIM support our quarterly dosing strategy. Estimated subcutaneous bioavailability was approximately 62% and PK modeling of our 400-milligram quarterly dosing regimen predicts a geometric mean ratio of exposure relative to IV BRIUMVI of 1.20 with a lower bound of the 90% confidence interval that exceeds the non-inferiority threshold for success defined in our ongoing Phase III study. The pharmacodynamic findings were equally encouraging. All patients receiving the fully subcutaneous 400-milligram regimen achieved B-cell depletion within four days with depletion maintained throughout the dosing intervals. Importantly, the 400-milligram subcu injections were well tolerated with limited local and systemic injection-related reactions observed, all of which were grade one.

The Phase III study of subcu BRIUMVI is fully enrolled with top line results expected around year-end or early 2027. Assuming successful development and regulatory review, we continue to target a potential commercial launch in 2028. Lastly, turning to azer-cel, our allogeneic CD19-directed CAR T cell therapy, we presented the first clinical results from our Phase I progressive MS study in a late-breaking oral presentation at ATRS. The initial data set included 26 patients with progressive MS, all of whom had experienced disability progression despite high efficacy treatment, including prior anti-CD20 therapy. The median baseline EDSS score was 6.0, reflecting a population with substantial accumulated disability.

The early safety findings were encouraging with no dose-limiting toxicities observed across all dose levels, no Grade 3 or higher CRS, no grade 2 or higher ICANS, no GvHD and no grade 3 or higher infections observed. From a pharmacodynamic perspective, 25 of 26 patients achieved peripheral B-cell depletion, and there was early evidence of reduced B cell counts in cerebrospinal fluid, a compartment generally inaccessible to current anti-CD20 therapy. Turning to the preliminary clinical findings. At day 90 post CAR-T administration, nearly 90% of evaluable patients had stable or improved EDSS scores with the longest follow-up patients sustaining a two-point reduction for 1.5 years in counting.

While early, these observations are encouraging, particularly in a population with documented disability progression despite previous high efficacy therapy. We continue to follow these patients to assess longer-term outcomes while advancing dose optimization and look forward to sharing additional updates as the data mature. Finally, we continue to advance BRIUMVI into additional therapeutic areas beyond MS. Our Phase II study in generalized myasthenia gravis is evaluating whether rapid disease control with FcRn inhibition followed by BRIUMVI maintenance can provide more durable benefit while reducing the burden of ongoing treatment. This study has generated a lot of excitement as it explores a novel way to sequence therapies in MG to maximize their benefit.

We are also conducting an exploratory Phase II study in treatment-resistant schizophrenia to investigate whether B-cell depletion can provide clinical benefit in a patient population where emerging evidence suggests immune dysfunction may contribute to disease biology. Both programs are designed to generate meaningful clinical evidence with a disciplined approach to development investment and additional programs in other therapeutic areas are also under development. Looking ahead, the next several years will be an important period across our development programs, and our team remains focused on executing against these opportunities. With that, I'll turn the call over to our Chief Commercial Officer, Adam Waldman, for a commercial update.

Adam Waldman: Thank you, Hari, and good morning, everyone. We continue to build on BRIUMVI's commercial success with broader physician adoption and a growing base of patients on treatment. As Mike noted, third quarter U.S. BRIUMVI net revenue reached approximately $233 million, our 14th consecutive quarter of sequential growth. And as we discussed on our last call, we expected second half growth to be primarily driven by the fourth quarter, which is exactly what we're seeing.

With our core business metrics continuing to strengthen and a projected strong fourth quarter, we are raising our BRIUMVI U.S. net product revenue guidance from $890 million to $905 million to a new range of $915 million to $920 million, reflecting more than $260 million for the fourth quarter which takes the U.S. BRIUMVI business above $1 billion annualized revenue run rate for the first time. Behind these results, we continue to see progress across our key commercial priorities. BRIUMVI is strengthening its competitive position and has become an increasingly important choice in the MS market. As Mike and Hari discussed, our long-term and real-world data are helping physicians better understand BRIUMVI's differentiated profile.

These findings reinforce what physicians are seeing in practice and give them more reasons to consider BRIUMVI for their patients. We believe that combination of evidence and experience is building confidence and contributing to broader adoption. New patient starts continue to grow year-over-year, and we have seen an acceleration at the end of Q3 and continuing into Q4. Persistence remains strong. We're seeing a steady flow of new prescribers along with continued growth in repeat prescribing with October being a record for total BRIUMVI prescribers in a month. Our hospital business also delivered encouraging growth during the quarter. September and October were our strongest hospital months since launch.

We've consistently viewed the hospitals as an important opportunity, and we're beginning to see the benefits of the sustained effort we've made in this segment. Together, these trends are expanding our installed base of patients returning approximately every six months for treatment. And as that installed base grows, it creates an increasingly durable and predictable foundation of recurring revenue. We're also seeing an important evolution in where BRIUMVI fits in the treatment journey. Treatment-naive patients now represent approximately 40% of our new patient business compared with approximately 25% at launch. We're also seeing increasing adoption among younger women ages 18 to 40. This is an important shift.

It tells us that physicians are increasingly comfortable choosing BRIUMVI as an initial high-efficacy treatment rather than waiting until a patient has experience with another therapy. At the same time, approximately 1/3 of our new patient starts continue to come from patients transitioning from another CD20 therapy, a portion that has remained remarkably stable since launch. What's particularly encouraging is that we continue to attract these patients even as the competitive landscape evolves, including efforts by other manufacturers to transition patients from their IV to subcutaneous formulation. Taken together, these trends demonstrate the increasing relevance of BRIUMVI, both as an initial treatment choice and as an option for patients considering a change in therapy.

We're also beginning to see the benefits of the commercial investments we've made. Our expanded field organization is contributing to growth in new patient starts, by increasing educational efforts with established prescribers and expanding our reach among physicians with less BRIUMVI experience. Complementing that field effort, our direct-to-consumer initiatives are building awareness and confidence in BRIUMVI and encouraging conversations with health care providers. We're now seeing measurable results, including increases in aided and unaided awareness and prescription lift associated with our campaigns. We're also investing in data analytics and AI-enabled tools to improve field targeting, personalized physician education and help us deploy our commercial resources more effectively.

Our objective is straightforward: to support continued growth while increasing the productivity and scalability of our commercial organization. Looking ahead, we see two important opportunities to significantly expand the BRIUMVI franchise. The first is the simplified IV single-dose initiation regimen. We see this as more than an incremental enhancement. And importantly, we believe we're particularly well positioned to capture this opportunity with an established brand, broad physician awareness and existing commercial infrastructure, we have the potential to generate substantial new revenue without having to build an entirely new commercial organization. In summary, we continue to build momentum. With future opportunities to strengthen IV and a potential multibillion-dollar opportunity in self-administered treatment, we see substantial growth ahead.

Immunovant (IMVT) Q2 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Immunovant drops Sjögren's and points to 2027 readouts.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Immunovant, Inc. (IMVT +15.13%) reported that its lead candidate, IMVT-1402, met the primary endpoint in a Phase 2 trial for difficult-to-treat rheumatoid arthritis, with the 600 mg dose achieving a 92.5% ACR20 response at week 28. Management indicated a strategic decision to deprioritize further development in Sjögren’s disease, citing unfavorable clinical data from competitors and the evolving market landscape. Parent company Roivant Sciences reported a commercial launch for LISRAYA, yielding $31.0 million in initial revenue and broad early physician adoption. The company confirmed it is on track for major data readouts in Graves’ disease and myasthenia gravis in 2027 while maintaining a balance sheet intended to fund operations through its first potential commercial launch.

In Period 2, those patients who had achieved an ACR20 response were then put into a randomized withdrawal portion, where they were either kept on 600 mg or randomized down to 300 mg or placebo. These patients on slide 12 have significant morbidity and quality of life impairment. A significant portion of them are fully work disabled for over a decade. Similar disease severity, similar balance of prior meds, et cetera. A pretty well-balanced study. I think what we saw on Slide 15 was just phenomenal across a couple of dimensions.

Almost all of them, 92.5%, still had an ACR20 response at the end of 28 weeks, whereas only 75%-ish had an ACR20 response on placebo. Notably, that got a p-value for the 600 mg arm. 300 mg looked pretty similar to placebo, which I think is just a further reinforcement of something we've believed all along, which is that depth of IgG suppression really matters across FcRn indications, and that it took a higher dose with deeper IgG suppression to deliver the sustained clinical benefit in this patient population. You can see on slide 16, similarly great data on ACR50 and ACR70. This is the cohort of patients who were on 600 mg for the full period, and you can see already some meaningful ACR50 and ACR70 responses as early as week 4, and those responses really continue to get better and are well-preserved through the end of the study, even though after week 16, there starts to be a, "placebo effect", where some of these patients were where the patients thought they might have been taken off drug at that point. This data looks great, and in my opinion, supports a clinically meaningful profile for these patients that is pretty exciting.

You can see on slide 18 just a little bit more data here on separation from placebo on CDAI and SDAI, which reflect widely used scales in clinical practice for assessing sustained response. You can see these placebo patients really worsened, whereas the drug patients were able to preserve their response through week 28, which is pretty exciting. The other thing I'll just add on slide 19 is looking at the JAK experience subset. The JAK experience subset did just about as well as the overall population. Even in these patients who have failed really the most effective anti-inflammatory mechanisms available in RA, we had really nice continued preserved responses, which feels good as well.

Same thing on slide 20 in the deeper response levels, ACR50 and ACR70. Data looked good even among JAK failures. Safety on slide 21 was entirely consistent with what we've shared before, consistent with the mechanism. Event rates comparable to placebo. Everything sort of looked reasonable. No new safety signals. 1402 continues to look safe and well-tolerated as a drug, which is great for all of the ongoing programs that we have. We had hoped, on Slide 22, to be able to share together with this update, that we were through the FDA discussions and had a path forward. Those discussions are ongoing. Frankly, we had to disclose this data at this point because we hit a p-value unexpectedly.

We will come back to you once we have finished our FDA discussions, probably later this year or early next year, with an update on our trial plans. We think, based on this data, we have a really exciting set of opportunities here to treat a patient population with a high unmet need, where the Period 2 data really support deep therapeutic responses in a population that has failed multiple mechanisms, multiple advanced therapies. Excited to come back and think this is going to be one of the important pillars for 1402 potentially as a product.

I am not going to go through the next two sections in great detail, but because they are both transformative updates for us, even though we have gotten the call for, I wanted to remind everybody of what we have seen both in NIU and in PH-ILD. It was just a few weeks ago we got on the phone together to talk about our NIU data. Again, just tremendously proud of what this has meant for us clinically in terms of, brepo continues to do basically everything that we could ask for it as an agent. NIU is a highly morbid disease, on Slide 24. It is a poorly served indication. It is the third leading cause of blindness.

There are hundreds of thousands of patients with anterior uveitis, and then potentially hundreds of thousands of patients, or at least we thought 70,000 to 190,000 patients with posterior intermediate or panuveitis. That is obviously a specific target population here. The data from CLARITY, as a reminder on slide 25, really suggests we can achieve a new standard of care here, as compared with placebo patients who failed therapy in around 12 weeks across the two studies.

We did not see median treatment failure in this patient population in over 48 weeks, which is a phenomenal, I think it is the largest benefit ever seen for a non-steroidal therapy in NIU, in that it met the primary endpoint and all secondary endpoints in both of our studies, with almost two-thirds of patients achieving steroid-free quiescence, which is a major treatment goal for physicians. Consistent across all subgroups, statistically and clinically meaningful, generally well-tolerated. Look, this data has been incredibly well-received by the doc community as we have been out talking about it. I think it is going to be an important new treatment option for NIU patients.

We are going to spend a fair amount of time on our Investor Day in December talking about the marketplace for NIU and the commercial opportunity here, so I will not belabor the point here, but really looking forward to talking about that, as I think NIU is going to be another pillar, hopefully as exciting as DM, which given the earnings results today, is a high bar to clear. Really exciting. Again, not going to go through the data slide by slide, but we have reproduced it here because we are quite proud of it. Same thing with mosliciguat, jumping to Slide 31. As a reminder, PH-ILD is a really tough disease with few current treatment options.

These patients have one and a half to two years median survival despite best available standard of care therapy. We've said about up to 200,000 patients across the U.S. and Europe. It's likely an under-reported disease. You see the market growing as new therapies like Tyvaso are on the market, and there are no non-treprostinil approved therapies for these patients, so there's a big opportunity to deliver something new. Don't need to belabor the data, but on Slide 32, we were just tremendously proud of what mosliciguat was able to do for these patients. On the primary endpoint of PVR, we saw a 56% placebo-adjusted PVR reduction at week 16.

That is, we think, the deepest PVR ever shown, certainly in a PH-ILD study. We showed a 35 m statistically significant improvement in the key secondary, a six-minute walk at week 16. On multiple week 24 exploratory analyses, we saw tremendous outcomes, including a meaningful benefit on NT-proBNP and a phenomenal benefit on six-minute walk at week 24. Cardiac measures, the sort of hemodynamics, looked phenomenal, and 98% of patients achieved the high dose, which is a good signal of safety and tolerability. And notably, given the tolerability profile of treprostinil, we saw well-tolerated cough rates that were lower than placebo, which is something that's important for these patients with lung disease.

Not going to go through it slide by slide here, but we reproduced the data again because we're just tremendously proud of what mosliciguat's been able to demonstrate in this patient population. Just phenomenal. On Slide 37, as a reminder, that phase III study is underway, actively screening and enrolling patients. Excited to continue to provide updates on that, including, based on the quality of this data, we've said multiple times, and we really mean it, this is a drug that we think is going to work in a lot of places, and we're excited to share updates in the coming months on initiation of other trials with mosliciguat in other indications, where we are now hard at work.

I will wrap up here with just a quick financial update on Slide 39. Relatively consistent with expectations in terms of expenses for the quarter. Net of tax, loss from continuing operations of $153 million, or non-GAAP of $133 million. Cash is back at $4.2 billion as of September 30, reflecting in part the receipts from the Moderna litigation that we got over the summer. In the six months ended 9/30, we had repurchased about $280 million worth of stock, about 9.4 million shares.

Look, on Slide 41, 2026 has been a tough year to beat for us, just in terms of the phenomenal quantum of clinical data, the meaningfulness of that clinical data, and now with the LISRAYA launch off to a start that we're pretty excited about. But 2027's a very busy year. In addition to getting the sNDA file for NIU and hopefully adding another indication in relatively short order for brepo, we have some very important top-line data coming for 1402 in Graves', some data in MG. We expect multiple program indication expansion, just a lot of other things coming, including some hopeful surprises over that time, so looking forward to next year.

Looking forward to seeing many of you in New York for our Investor Day next month. I think we've got a lot to come. With that, I will pause to just remind everybody, our Investor Day is on December 9th. Please register. The link is in the presentation from today. I will hand it back to the operator to start Q&A. Thank you again, everybody. I want to just, before I do that, just say thank you again to everybody who makes this happen, the Roivant employees, the Vant employees, Priovant, Immunovant, Pulmovant, great updates from all those teams, and then obviously, again, to the patients and investigators who trust us with their care. It has been a phenomenal year.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question is going to come from Dave Risinger with Leerink Partners.

David Risinger: Congrats, Matt, to you and the team on a phenomenal quarter. My question is on LISRAYA. Could you talk about the evolution of paid RX, just to help us understand what percentage of RXs were paid for in the September quarter, and as of early November, what percentage are paid for today? And then regarding the scripts, what are you seeing in terms of the mix of RX that are switches from off-label JAKs versus switches from IVIg?

Matthew Gline: Yes, perfect. First of all, just as a reminder on the way that we do reporting, our bridge program is not reported as sales in any way, and so it is really everything in that number is, quote, unquote, paid, although obviously it is paid at the time it is purchased by the pharmacy. I will say, without giving specific numbers, we are still in the early innings of payer coverage, and the early innings of payer coverage have been straightforward, and so we are getting very good conversion rates at this point, with relatively straightforward access from a payer dynamic.

Obviously, the concern or the question is, as the payers get their act together, we will start to see plans in place, and we have seen some of those programs in place or access controls in place, and we have seen some of that. I will say it has ranged from, there are significant national plans whose only restriction is that you have to have tried a systemic immunosuppressant. Then, there are plans that are trying more significant restrictions than that, and I think it will be a variety, and I think we are prepared to help every patient get access to drug.

The hundreds that I indicated as of 9/30 and the many hundreds that I indicated as of now are all on paid drug, having made it through that process. That is sort of how we are thinking about those numbers. I think feeling good. I would say there has not so far been a significant change in access relative to early in the launch. Maybe like reading tea leaves, small changes up or down at different times, but really nothing significant so far. Access continues to be pretty straightforward for the moment.

I do not have a lot of specific things to report in terms of who is coming on drug, other than to say, we had originally indicated that we thought it was going to be quite a broad patient population. I think we are, in fact, seeing a broad patient population. It continues to be prescriber-specific which patients are coming on. There are prescribers who are moving patients from off-label JAKs or from IVIg. There are prescribers who are moving patients from steroids and immunosuppressants. Look, it is a great option for patients, and a lot of patients and physicians are enthusiastic about it. There are even some newly diagnosed patients coming on to drug.

So I think we are seeing a pretty broad variety of uptake, and it really is varying by practice and is hitting the whole spectrum in terms of who we might get.

Operator: The next question will come from Sam Slutsky with LifeSci Capital.

Samuel Slutsky: Congrats on the great updates. I guess on just the RA study, could you just remind us on the IgG reduction differences between 600 mg and 300 mg you saw there? Then, I realize it's early, but any sensitivity analysis you're able to do even within the 600 mg cohort for those who had deeper versus less?

Matthew Gline: Yes. Perfect. It's a great question. This was a tremendously exciting data. We have not shared IgG or antibody data in this study because what we've learned is this field is competitive, and everything we do gets closely followed. Also, as you saw from our data, it's clear to us that we have a competitive advantage by being able to more deeply suppress IgG and autoantibody levels, and we're trying to preserve that advantage as best possible. As a reminder, in the phase I study, we saw pushing high 70s IgG reduction at 600 mg.

You can see in this data that indeed the 600 mg dose outperformed the 300 mg dose on the primary and secondary endpoints, which is consistent with deeper IgG suppression of the kind we saw in the phase I study mattering here. So we're feeling pretty good about that. I think we have learned a lot of interesting things. Both to your question from specifically from sensitivity analyses around IgG suppression among the data, the data is certainly consistent with the thesis that deeper reduction leads to better outcomes. There's a variety of other sensitivity analysis we've done that is also helpful in informing how we think the drug is working, what we think it's doing.

Remember, there's 170 patients overall, 118 in Period 2. This was consistent across multiple endpoints. I think that just about covers it.

Operator: The next question will come from Yaron Werber with TD Cowen.

Yaron Werber: Great. Congrats on really a terrific, amazing quarter all around. Maybe just a quick couple. Is there inventory for LISRAYA this quarter? Can you quantify it? Secondly, I know you're obviously continuing your discussion with FDA on imeroprubart 1402. Any sense that whether just one phase III will be sufficient for approval? With the endpoint, one would presume is going to be longer than 16 weeks.

Matthew Gline: Yes. So on the inventory question, I think the way to think about this, again, all of the sales that we book are sales to specialty pharmacy partners. As I think I mentioned, there were hundreds of patients on paid drug that is sort of dispensed fills as of the 9/30 quarter. There was a meaningful amount of undispensed drug that specialty pharmacies were holding as of 9/30. All of what they were holding at that point has now been dispensed, and there continues to be sort of further ordering. I think we saw a tailwind from those dynamics in the 9/30 quarter.

I think there may be a very modest headwind from those dynamics in the 12/31 quarter, but mostly I don't think this is going to be a significant contributor to the variability going forward. I think those inventory builds were largely driven by demand. And there's no inventory requirements in our specialty pharmacy agreements, and we ship when people order. On the RA question, look, I think the honest answer to your question is we don't know on either of those questions for sure, that is whether one phase III will be sufficient or what's the endpoint.

We think this is a population with high unmet need and not a lot of options, and so we're going to talk to FDA about a relatively aggressive plan, and we're hoping to meet a reasonable reaction just given, A, the quality of this dataset, and B, the level of unmet need. And frankly, the fact that this study hit a p-value is certainly helpful, as well as a part of that discussion, this data is good. I think, overall, we're hopeful for a good reaction there, but there's still some uncertainty until we've aligned with FDA, including on things like endpoints. So, looking forward to a further discussion once we know that.

Operator: The next question will come from Thomas Smith with Leerink Partners.

Thomas Smith: Congrats on the strong RA results, and thanks so much for taking our questions. A couple on 1402. Just wondering, given the strength of the results in this really difficult-to-treat patient population, any thoughts or plans to expand the development program beyond the 85,000 addressable refractory patients? Is that something that could perhaps be discussed within the context of the upcoming regulatory engagement? Then, also just wondering on the current Period 2 data, I know there's a four-week safety follow-up. Just wondering if there's any potential or opportunity to continue monitoring patients in that four-week follow-up to see how the response rates evolve with greater follow-up.

Matthew Gline: Those are both great questions. The first one, I confess, has a what have you done for me lately flavor, and that we just reported great data focused on this patient population. Look, I think we are very focused on, first and foremost, getting this drug out to these patients. There are a lot of them. Their unmet need is high. They are patients who have a demonstrated willingness to try multiple therapies and have failed the ones they have tried. I think, first and foremost, we want to get out there.

Obviously, as we continue to learn more about how FcRns work in these immune complex diseases and diseases that have more complicated pathobiology, I think we are thinking about places to go that could include other subsets of RA patients. It could include other diseases. We have some good ideas. But again, first and foremost, we really want to get out to this population. I think in terms of what we are going to learn for evolution of responses from this continued data, I think we have already learned an enormous amount from this study. I think we will continue to learn a little bit as we continue to see what is going on in this study.

More importantly, I think we just want to get the phase III program up and running, because I think this is going to be a big benefit to patients, and we got to get going. I will note that we were aware of one other program in late-stage studies in this patient population from Artiva, and obviously that program was not able to proceed for safety reasons. We think the unmet need looks even more urgent today than it did not very long ago, and it is a reminder of just what FcRn is able to deliver in terms of the risk-benefit trade-off, and we hope that is going to continue in this disease. Thank you, Tom.

Operator: The next question will come from Dennis Ding with Jefferies.

Yuchen Ding: Congrats on a fantastic quarter. I have a question on LISRAYA. It is tough to square the math for me between the hundreds of patients on paid drug that you reported and the $31 million that is booked. I know you guys will not disclose a specific inventory revenue number, but is it fair to say that the majority of the revenue booked came from inventory? Then, remind me how many patients from your phase III were in the U.S., and who converted to commercial drug in the quarter, but also the pace of conversion.

Matthew Gline: Yes. Look, I think the truth is we are not going to break out the specifics of how these numbers add up right now, in part because remember, LISRAYA was approved in late August, and so you are talking about five weeks in total. Frankly, the pace of conversion from RX to paid RX is such that one-day difference or a few days' difference in terms of when the quarter happened can make a big difference in how these numbers add up, which is obviously irrelevant to the long-term trajectory.

I think it is just not that meaningful to draw the line in the sand, other than to reiterate again, there was a meaningful amount of drug held by the pharmacies at the end of the quarter, and it has all been dispensed now, and demand continues to be very good. There were tens of patients from the phase III in the U.S., so I think that is the mechanical answer to that question. Of those, there was no U.S. EAP. There was no sort of defined path to get on commercial drug. There is no sort of EAP transition effect in this data, no sort of bolus of patients coming from the trial or anything like that.

A meaningful percentage of those patients are on drug. Some are not yet on drug. In many cases, there was a pretty significant gap between the end of the study and when the drug got approved. This is, I think, clear from the numbers that there is an order of magnitude more patients on drug than the entire number of U.S. patients from the OLE. So it is just not a meaningful driver of any of this.

Operator: The next question is going to come from Brian Cheng with JPMorgan.

Brian Cheng: Matt, do you have any color in terms of the number of touchpoints you have had with the DM specialists, and how many of them have been converted and actively prescribing with LISRAYA? One more on RA. Just giving the slight difference in the baseline CDAI score between 600 mg and placebo, how should we think about the potential of it influencing the efficacy output?

Matthew Gline: Yes. Look, on the first, we have many hundreds of prescribers at this point, which is awesome. It is just a phenomenal number in terms of the number of people who have written. Again, I think it is a reflection of the level of enthusiasm. The Priovant team is excellent at many things. One of the things they are excellent at is pounding pavement. I do not have a number, but we have had lots of touchpoints with the DM specialists, and I think that has been great.

I think it has been an important moment for the field, and I think we have been out there from a med affairs perspective, we have been out there from a commercial perspective. I think you see it even this weekend at the conference. There is just a lot of enthusiasm for brepo, and we are excited to be continuing to talk about the drug in every setting that we are able. Anyway, that is it on the brepo question. On 1402, I think the short answer to that is not much to read into on CDAI. Remember that because it is a randomized withdrawal trial, it is not exactly obvious which direction is better.

A higher starting point could be better or easier, but it is a little bit unclear. As a reminder, all of these scores are actually positively biased by the fact that these patients were on drug for 16 weeks and were limited to the responders. I think it is a little bit difficult to read in exactly to the meaning of that number. But overall, I do not think anything that we have seen, anything notable from that sort of relatively small delta across the arms. The numbers are strong and consistent across the board, and I think it is just about overall clinical benefit.

Operator: The next question is going to come from Alex Thompson with Stifel.

Patrick Culliton: Congrats on the quarter. This is Patrick on for Alex. Switching gears a little bit, I guess, could you guys just talk about, for mosli, what additional phase II starts we should maybe expect next year, or how you're thinking about prioritizing these other PH indications?

Matthew Gline: Yes. It's one that I'm personally really excited about, given what mosli was able to show in that PH-ILD study. Frankly, we're now reaping the benefit from having started that PH-ILD study ahead of time, in that the team has been able to start to turn focus to these other phase III study starts. I think what we've said in various settings before is that we were excited about IPF, that we were worried about competitive dynamics in PAH. I think our world sort of turned upside down in a great way once we saw the data. So I think what we've said is that every form of pulmonary hypertension is exciting to us now. We're aggressively looking at PAH.

We're looking at the other forms of pulmonary hypertension to see where there might be good opportunities. We're looking at IPF. We're looking at PPF. Lots of good places to go. I can't commit to any of those indications now. Some of them could be phase IIIs, some of them might be phase IIs, depending on the indication. But I think we're envisioning a pretty broad program, and we're sprinting to the starting line on additional indications. So looking forward to talking about it as soon as we can.

Operator: Our next question will come from Yasmeen Rahimi with Piper Sandler.

Yasmeen Rahimi: Congrats on an amazing year, and more to come for next year. I guess my question is, 2027 is right around the corner. It could be a very big year for Immunovant with Graves' and MG data. Obviously, on ClinicalTrials.gov, these studies are still indicated as recruiting. They're 26 weeks long. Just would love to get an idea at what point over the next few months would you be in a position to fine-tune guidance, provide color, and maybe even in this call, provide commentary on the enrollment to help us understand the timing of these two studies, specifically around Graves'. Appreciate it.

Matthew Gline: I appreciate it. I will say enrollment has been strong in Graves'. I think we benefited from pioneering that field and being first. I do not have an update to share today, but I expect to have one relatively soon on timing for next year and how everything goes. So, looking forward to sharing that in the relatively near future.

Operator: The next question is going to come from Derek Archila with Wells Fargo.

Unknown Analyst: Congrats on all the updates. Just one from us on difficult-to-treat RA. Could you comment on what you saw from the degree of ACPA positivity or autoantibody levels relative to IgG? Then, given what you saw in the II-B, would you expect the same ACPA positivity criteria to get carried forward into the phase III? Thanks.

Matthew Gline: On the autoantibody side, I will say I think we have learned interesting, exciting things that are highly competitively valuable, so we are going to say almost nothing about autoantibody reduction for that reason. What I will say is, I think based on what we have learned, I think we have got a good amount of confidence going into phase III. I do not think we intend to make a significant change to our enrollment criteria, but again, we have not finished that conversation with FDA, so we are still working through the details of that, and there could be changes in one direction or another depending on how that goes.

But overall, feeling good about our plan going forward and feeling like I mean, honestly, and kudos to the various teams here who have worked on it. I think we have really found a patient population that is well-suited to this therapy, and we are excited to carrying forward in that patient population given what we have seen today.

Operator: The next question will come from Samantha Semenkow with Citi.

Samantha Semenkow: And let me add my congrats on your very strong quarter. Just a question on 1402. As you've highlighted in the RA data, it seems that the greater IgG suppression is necessary to drive that difference versus placebo, and this is just the latest dataset where you've seen this pattern. I'm wondering just how are you thinking about the Sjögren's opportunity again in this context, even given the recent competitor data? Thanks very much.

Matthew Gline: And obviously the J&J Sjögren's study looked like there was a dose response as well. We said today we're probably not expecting to progress Sjögren's. The truth is, argenx's futility analysis had a really low bar, and they failed in 500 patients, which is just a tough sign. Among other reasons, one of the reasons we're providing an update today is, in order to meet the timelines we'd originally set for ourselves, our plan had either been to expand the existing phase II or to add a phase III on right about now, and I think it just doesn't make sense to do that given what we know.

So, look, we're hoping to learn as much as we can from our phase II to finish the study. Obviously, if there's something surprising, we'll reevaluate, but just given the experience of our competitors and what we've seen in different directions, including Novartis's ongoing discussions with the FDA, what we've seen from Amgen, et cetera, we're just thinking it's relatively unlikely at this point. We'll learn what we can from the phase II, and if there's something interesting, we'll come back.

Operator: The next question is going to come from Douglas Tsao at HC Wainwright.

Douglas Tsao: Matt, in terms of the RA, after the part one data, you sort of set an expectation or noted that it might be hard to see sort of a difference in part two. I'm just curious, given the fact that we did see some nice separation ultimately, what was sort of the key takeaway from you? Was it the rapidity that placebo patients sort of declined, or was it that the treatment effect sort of really continued to maintain itself? What does that tell you about the opportunity for you from a commercial standpoint?

Matthew Gline: It's a great question, and part of what is interesting is, again, you're thinking all of these patients come in with an ACR20. Three-quarters of them, 75% on placebo, have maintained an ACR20 response. So, there appears to be some sort of durability of clinical benefit, which is interesting. I think against the backdrop of 75% of these ACR20 responders still had a response at the end, I think the fact that we were able to preserve north of 90% of those responders on drug is pretty exciting, again, in a patient population that has really struggled across others.

So, I think we're pretty excited about both the sort of durability of off-drug effect as well as the durability of continuing on-drug effect and the fact that we saw a continued build in some of the responder rates, especially at ACR50 and ACR70 over time. I think it is just pretty interesting data overall, and we think that translates to an exciting commercial opportunity. Again, I am looking forward to --one of the things we are going to do on our Investor Day is spend some time digging in on this and why we are so excited about it. I will plant that as a flag for please come and listen. I think that will be a good session.

I think the data really did us a solid here.

Operator: The next question is coming from Ash Verma with UBS.

Ashwani Verma: Just on 1402 for difficult-to-treat RA. You mentioned the FDA interaction is the next step. Can you talk a little bit about the initial thoughts on what you think would be the right clinical trial design here? Is it likely a regimen that would be a combo with methotrexate or TNFs, or are you thinking of monotherapy? Just in terms of trial design, is it likely to be parallel or randomized withdrawal?

Matthew Gline: Look, I think the first thing is, the right study design here is the one that gets the drug approved, so that's ultimately got to be a conversation together with FDA. We think this population has a big effect. A lot of the particulars in terms of endpoint and so on are going to be discussions. I think it's relatively unlikely this will be a randomized withdrawal study. I think it's pretty likely, just given the division and the way other RA studies have worked, this will be a straightforward RCT.

I think other than that, in terms of patient population, it will be quite similar to what we've done here in the phase II-B in this study, because it's a good patient population. We expect a lot of collaboration from FDA, and we think we'll get to a path forward here. Again, I think the questions are end and specifics around endpoints and things like that. I think we're hoping for a reasonable dialogue with FDA on those points. There's a pretty broad range of potential outcomes depending on how FDA approaches the questions, and we're looking forward to sharing that once we've got it.

Operator: I am showing no further questions at this time. I will now turn the call back over to Matthew Gline for closing remarks.

Matthew Gline: Look, it's been a really fun year for us. I think there's no substitute in this business for generating clinical data that matters, and we've had a lot of opportunity to do that across multiple indications. It's tremendously rewarding when something like the LISRAYA approval and launch happens, where you plan for something for a long time, you work really hard as a team on getting it there, you generate data that matters for patients, FDA agrees with you, then you get to actually see patients on drug using it, physicians excited to make it a part of their practice. It's a really great moment, and it feels amazing.

Huge kudos to the Roivant team, to the Priovant team, to the Pulmovant team, the Immunovant team. These things are a ton of work, and even in the AI age, there is no substitute for hard work and pavement pounding, and it has been a lot of that. Then, again, just thank you to the patients in our studies who have made this possible, the investigators, and now to the patients and the physicians who are entrusting us with their care in dermatomyositis. It is a great moment for Roivant, and I am looking forward to lots of good stuff coming.

Thank you, everybody, and looking forward to seeing many of you in just a few short weeks here for our Investor Day. Have a great day.

Select Water (WTTR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Pilot Water and Peak Rentals moves reshape Select Water's outlook.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Select Water Solutions, Inc. (WTTR -6.86%) reported record operational performance for the first nine months of the year, driven by significant volume growth in its infrastructure segment. Management stated that the recent acquisition of Pilot Water expands the company's disposal capacity and complements its existing recycling network in the Delaware Basin. The company indicated that the divestment of a majority stake in Peak Rentals was a strategic move to concentrate resources on core water management and chemical technologies. Management noted that new contract expansions and acreage dedications are expected to provide a strong growth profile for contracted earnings heading into 2027.

Now, obviously, with the addition of Pilot, we are adding more fixed infrastructure, more customers, more contracts, and we think we can further commercialize those. I would say that in the past when we have lost an opportunity, it is usually been around our reluctance or inability to provide firm capacity on the disposal side. Obviously, Pilot, once we interconnect the system between the available capacity they have and the extensive permits of approved permits and undrilled capacity they have, that will largely resolve that issue.

And would the changing regulatory backdrop put any of your disposal capacity at risk? Or conversely, does it make permitted capacity more valuable? Just trying to think through how that could shake out.

Michael Skarke: Yeah, sure, Scott. This is Michael. Thanks for the question. I'd start off by saying that most importantly, we've got a very strong record of growing our business in highly regulated environments. So, when you look at kind of what we've been able to do, specifically in New Mexico, I think we're very well positioned to operate in stringent environments, from a recycling and disposal side, and just really partnering with the governing bodies.

In terms of disposal capacity, we do think that it puts a premium on disposal capacity, which is why we're so excited that we were able to close the Pilot acquisition when we did, because it comes with a considerable amount, almost 900,000 bbl a day of approved permitted capacity. That we could tap into and drill and expand our network to the extent that you have constraints on existing capacity or the demand to provide more firm capacity than what the existing network can do. In terms of the ability to pass along, that's an important component. Our contracts have change in law provisions that allow us to pass any sort of change in pricing along to the customer.

We feel like we're well-positioned in the event that we see meaningful changes in the regulatory environment. I would say, though, that in general, as you start to see change in regulations, it generally creates opportunities for solution-oriented service companies like Select. Overall, in summary, I'd say that we're really not expecting any material changes to the business, and to the extent that some come, we think we're very well-positioned to deal with them.

Scott Gruber: I appreciate all that color. Then maybe turn into Peak Rentals. Good to see the transaction that you guys have been contemplating for a while take place. Jeff Robertson: Thank you. Michael, can you talk about what you can do in 2027 to bring the Northern Delaware and the Southern Delaware Basin systems together so you can leverage the entire footprint of the company?

Michael Skarke: Sure, Jeff. I mean, that's really our goal, and I know we've said it, but that's what makes this consolidated platform so exciting, because the two systems are highly complementary from a geographic standpoint. They're not very far apart, but there's also not a lot of overlap. We're currently evaluating a number of different ways to tie in our primarily New Mexico large-diameter recycling-first solution with the Pilot system that exists in southern Lea County, but really goes throughout the Texas, Delaware.

It's not as simple as just running a pipeline from the southernmost portion of our system to the northernmost portion of theirs, which is why we're going through and looking at a couple of different ways to make sure that we're managing the hydraulics and tying in our large-diameter line with the northern part of their large-diameter line. I'd note that the large MVC that we signed earlier this year in the second quarter, it's taking our system down into Loving County. That's going to serve as one of the major arteries, and that asset becomes even more important as we look forward to tying in our system with Pilot's system.

Really, when you back up, the key here is we think we're going to have the largest system, and collectively, we think we'll be able to grow recycling because of the firm disposal capacity that we can now offer, and we think we can grow the firm disposal capacity because of the network and the recycling solutions we offer.

Chris George: I would add, fortunately, that from a timing standpoint, given the recency of some of the recent contracts and the build-out of that is going to take place over the next 12-18 months, we have been able to reassess the opportunity set and the approach of how we build that out to make sure that we can optimize the build-out and the interconnectivity with the Pilot system as part of that construction timeline over the next 18 months. It gives us the opportunity to reassess, maximize the value potential of how we put it together, and build that out in a manner that fits the combined basis of both systems over that timeframe.

Jeff Robertson: Do you anticipate the type of solutions that you can offer to customers on the legacy Pilot asset base for organic growth projects would have a similar margin profile to what you all have been so successful doing up in the Northern Delaware Basin?

Chris George: Yeah. From a margin standpoint, Jeff, we certainly expect the margin profile of the future development opportunities to look consistent with the overall segment. Obviously, there is a little bit of a swing factor with regards to skim oil, but as you put the two systems together, the ability to harvest that skim oil potential, improve the capture rates across the combined platform, we think will continue to improve. The way we underwrite these new contracts is generally going to be consistent, whether it is recycle or disposal or a pure pipeline project. We are generally underwriting all of those on a consistent basis in that 50%-60% margin profile, consistent with the current platform.

Chris George: I was just going to say, when we do put the two together, Jeff, we do think there's opportunities to create efficiency and improve the margin profile of the acquired assets as well. We think that's another area where you've got both revenue and cost synergy potential from what we acquired.

Jeff Robertson: Lastly, on the permitted disposal, do those permits have a shelf life where they might need to be renewed at some point in the future?

Michael Skarke: They do have a shelf life where they need to be renewed or extended, something that we're monitoring, and it's not something that is going to become a restriction at this point. We're thrilled to have them. It's going to be a big part of our solution as we go forward, because again, you need recycling. It is the most economic solution. It's the most friendly from a pore space perspective, but you're also going to need local disposal and distant disposal, and we're very focused on providing the full suite of services.

Operator: Our next question is from Sean Mitchell with Daniel Energy Partners. Please proceed.

Sean Mitchell: Hey, guys. Thanks for taking the question. Maybe a follow-on to Derrick's question around surfactants. We've heard several E&Ps talk about it on their earnings calls last week. That we really do think does set 2027 up to allow for more adoption over the overall industry. Some of the customers that we've been, I think, undertaking longer live testing programs with so far are already changing the behavior of their new well completions.

We think that's going to continue to translate through to a lot of fast adopters and fast followers from a customer standpoint. We feel like 2027 is really the year where it is going to start to accelerate, and the pace of that over the course of the year we will continue to see. But we would be very surprised if you did not see a lot of fast movement in the industry behind the

Michael Skarke: The only thing I would add is we think you are going to see some of the large operators continue to talk about it, about the success they are having as their well results come in, like Chris mentioned. And when you see some of the larger operators talk about that success, you are going to have everyone else follow pretty quickly, as Chris alluded to.

Chris George: A lot of the phone calls we are getting now are based on customers that are not using the technology today or seeing the results and want to learn more. That is going to continue to accelerate.

Sean Mitchell: Got it. Thanks for the color.

Operator: This concludes the question-and-answer session. I would like to turn the call back over to John Schmitz for any final comments.

John Schmitz: Thanks to everyone for joining the call. We appreciate your continued support and interest in learning more about Select Water Solutions. We look forward to speaking to you again next quarter.

What is Muse Ember? Meet Meta’s new low-cost AI model

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Booking a vacation sounds like one thing to hand off to an AI assistant, right up until it has to check the calendar, open a dozen tabs, and figure out whether the cheapest flight is still the cheapest once a carry-on is involved. Every one of those steps takes work, and when an AI agent is doing it, the cost can add up.

Meta has a new model built for that part of the job.

On Nov. 9, Meta's Superintelligence Labs introduced Muse Ember, which the company calls its smallest and most cost-efficient AI model yet. It's designed for the steps an agent might repeat dozens of times in a single assignment, like pulling details out of a document, calling another tool, or running a test after changing a line of code.

Muse is the app with the cute little avatar — named Jolly — that Meta has been promoting since September. The AI assistant can work across (some) apps with a user's permission. The app passed 5 million downloads in 22 days, and has already had many updates; last week, Meta started rolling out voice conversations and animated avatars for the assistant in the U.S. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Meta also uses the Muse name for a family of AI models. The company positions Muse Wonder as the model for its toughest problems and Muse Spark as a model for coding and other work that involves using tools. Ember is the cheaper option for repeatable tasks. Meta's pitch is that developers can use Wonder to plan a complicated job and hand off the individual steps to Ember. For now, Meta lists Ember as available through its Muse Code tool and developer API.

In early testing shared by Meta, cloud storage company Box said it used Ember to check contracts clause by clause against a company’s negotiation rules and assign an overall risk rating. Meta says the model can take in up to a million tokens at once, enough to work through large sets of documents, and can handle images, audio, and video alongside text. That gives developers room to build an agent that can read a scanned contract or pull details from a meeting recording.

The price is what makes Ember interesting. On Artificial Analysis's benchmark, Ember and Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 both rounded to a score of 36 at their highest reasoning settings. Ember cost about 14 cents per benchmark task, compared with 41 cents for Haiku, even though the two have the same standard rates of 10 cents per million input tokens and 50 cents per million output tokens. OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna scored 28 and cost about 15 cents per task at its highest setting.

In Meta's published results, Ember beat Haiku on a terminal coding test, while Haiku did better on a test that judged whether code changes were ready to merge. Meta added that it already has even cheaper models in training.

As the company continues to bet that AI assistants will take on more everyday tasks, developers will need an affordable way to handle all the little steps behind the scenes. A flight search, for example, can mean sorting through dozens of fares, each with its own rules. If Meta wants people to hand off that kind of chore every day, it has to make checking the carry-on policy cheap on its end, too.

Olivia Tauber is the deputy editor of digital culture, covering creators, media, movies, beauty, and more. Based in New York, her work has appeared in The New York Times, Vanity Fair, The Cut, Teen Vogue, Complex, and Interview Magazine. Turkcell (TKC) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Fintech and fiber growth lifted results, though data center demand slowed.
